title: Parsing & Dispatching Tool Calls
summary: When the model wants to act, it returns a structured tool_calls field: each entry has a unique id, a tool name, and JSON arguments. Your job is to read that list, dispatch each call to the right Python function via a registry, execute it (validating arguments and catching errors), and append a tool-result message keyed by the matching call id — for every call, including several in one turn. Get the id pairing right and the model can follow exactly which observation answers which request.

subtopics.title: Read tool_calls from the response
subtopics.explanation: When the model decides to act, the response carries a tool_calls list instead of (or alongside) final content; each entry names a tool and supplies arguments and a unique id. Your loop branches on whether this list is non-empty. Reading tool_calls correctly is the entry point to the entire act phase — miss it and the model's requests are ignored.

subtopics.title: Arguments arrive as JSON to parse
subtopics.explanation: Most providers deliver tool-call arguments as a JSON string, not a ready Python dict, so you json.loads them before use, and you must tolerate malformed JSON. Parsing defensively — catching a decode error and turning it into an error observation — keeps one bad generation from crashing the loop. Treating arguments as untrusted JSON is the first safety step in dispatch.

subtopics.title: Dispatch to the right function via the registry
subtopics.explanation: With a parsed name and arguments, you look the function up in a name→callable registry and invoke it with the arguments. Guarding for an unknown name (the model can hallucinate a tool) turns a would-be crash into a recoverable error observation. Centralized dispatch is what keeps the loop generic no matter how many tools you add.

subtopics.title: Append a tool-result message keyed by call id
subtopics.explanation: Each observation must go back as a message with role 'tool' and the same tool_call_id the model used, so the model can match this result to the specific request it made. The id is the join key between a request and its answer. Correct id pairing is essential the moment the model issues more than one call in a turn.
subtopics.example:
result = dispatch(call["name"], args)
messages.append({
    "role": "tool",
    "tool_call_id": call["id"],   # MUST match the request's id
    "content": str(result),
})
# the model now knows THIS observation answers THAT call

subtopics.title: Handle multiple tool calls in one turn
subtopics.explanation: A single model turn can request several tools at once, so you iterate the whole tool_calls list, dispatching and appending a result for each before calling the model again. Skipping any call leaves a dangling request the model expected an answer to. Handling every call in the turn — one result per id — is what keeps the conversation well-formed for the next step.
subtopics.example:
# model asked for two tools in one turn
for call in resp.tool_calls:
    args = parse_args(call)
    result = dispatch(call["name"], args)
    messages.append({"role": "tool",
                     "tool_call_id": call["id"],
                     "content": str(result)})
# every id got exactly one tool-result message
next_resp = client.chat(messages, tools=TOOL_SCHEMAS)

foundations.overview: The act phase of the agent loop is really a parse-and-dispatch problem. When the model wants to use tools, its response carries a tool_calls list: each entry has a unique id, a tool name, and arguments that most providers deliver as a JSON string. Your code reads that list, parses each argument blob (defensively, because malformed JSON and hallucinated fields happen), looks the tool name up in a name→callable registry, executes the function, and appends a tool-result message back into the conversation. The single most important detail is the id: the tool-result message must carry the same tool_call_id the model used, because that id is the join key the model relies on to match each observation to the request that produced it. This matters especially when a single turn contains several tool calls — you must produce exactly one result message per id and skip none, or the conversation becomes ill-formed and the model gets confused about which answer belongs to which request. Wrapping dispatch so unknown tools and tool exceptions become plain-text error observations (rather than crashes) keeps the loop resilient and lets the model recover.
foundations.formalDefinition: Tool-call dispatch is the procedure that, given a model response containing a tool_calls list [(id, name, arguments)], for each entry parses arguments (typically json.loads of a string), resolves name against a registry of callables, executes callable(**arguments), and appends a message {role: 'tool', tool_call_id: id, content: result} to the history, producing exactly one result message per call id, with unknown names and execution errors converted to error observations.
foundations.whyItMatters: Dispatch is where the model's intent becomes real-world effect, and it's where a class of subtle bugs lives: mismatched or missing tool_call_ids, unparsed argument strings, and unhandled exceptions that halt the loop. Getting dispatch right — one validated, id-matched result per call, errors fed back as observations — is what makes a tool-using agent both correct and resilient.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a mail room. The model drops off several addressed request slips (each with a tracking id). You open each slip, read the request (parse arguments), route it to the right department (registry dispatch), get the reply, and mail it back stapled to the same tracking id (tool_call_id). If you lose a slip or swap the tracking ids, the sender can't tell which reply answers which request.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every function-calling agent runs this dispatch step: a coding agent parses a read_file call's path argument and returns the file contents keyed by the call id; a support agent dispatches get_order then, in the same turn, issue_refund, returning two results; a data agent parses a run_query argument and returns rows or an error observation.
foundations.performanceImpact: Handling multiple calls per turn in one pass reduces model round-trips versus forcing one tool per turn, directly cutting latency and cost. Parsing and dispatch overhead is negligible next to a model call, but converting errors to observations (instead of retrying blindly) avoids extra wasted turns.
commonUseCases: Reading and iterating a model's tool_calls list
Dispatching tool names to functions via a registry
Pairing tool-result messages to call ids across multiple calls

commonMisconceptions.myth: Tool-call arguments arrive as a ready Python dict.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Most providers send arguments as a JSON string you must json.loads, and it can be malformed, so you parse defensively.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can return one combined result for several tool calls.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Each call id needs its own tool-result message; the model matches observations to requests by id, so a combined or missing result breaks the pairing.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An error in a tool should crash the loop.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Wrap execution and feed the error text back as the tool result; the model can then recover, reroute, or report — a crash ends the run needlessly.

codeLab.title: Build the parse-and-dispatch step
codeLab.instructions: Implement handle_tool_calls(tool_calls, registry) -> list that returns a list of tool-result messages, one per call, in order. For each call: (1) parse its 'arguments' with json.loads if it is a string (else use it as-is); on a JSONDecodeError produce a result of "error: bad arguments"; (2) look the tool name up in `registry` — if missing, result is f"error: unknown tool '{name}'"; (3) otherwise call the function with the parsed args as **kwargs, and if it raises, result is f"error: {exception}"; (4) build a message {role: 'tool', tool_call_id: call['id'], content: str(result)}. Return the messages list. The harness passes valid, unknown-tool, and raising cases.

codeLab.testHarness:
def add(a, b): return a + b
def boom(): raise ValueError("nope")
registry = {"add": add, "boom": boom}

calls = [
    {"id": "1", "name": "add", "arguments": '{"a": 2, "b": 3}'},
    {"id": "2", "name": "nope", "arguments": '{}'},
    {"id": "3", "name": "boom", "arguments": '{}'},
    {"id": "4", "name": "add", "arguments": 'not json'},
]
out = handle_tool_calls(calls, registry)
assert [m["tool_call_id"] for m in out] == ["1", "2", "3", "4"]
assert out[0]["content"] == "5"
assert out[1]["content"] == "error: unknown tool 'nope'"
assert out[2]["content"] == "error: nope"
assert out[3]["content"] == "error: bad arguments"
print("all tests passed")

Use registry.get(name) and guard None so an unknown tool is a recoverable error, not a KeyError.
Every branch must still append one message keyed by call['id'] so the ids line up one-to-one.

theory.question: Walk through how you parse and dispatch a model's tool calls.
theory.directAnswer: Read the response's tool_calls list; for each entry parse its arguments (usually a JSON string, so json.loads defensively), resolve the tool name against a name→callable registry, execute the function with those arguments while catching exceptions, and append a tool-result message with role 'tool' and the same tool_call_id the model used. Do this for every call in the turn, producing exactly one id-matched result per call, and convert unknown tools and errors into error observations rather than crashing.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The act phase of the agent loop: turning the model's structured tool requests into function executions and observations.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The model emits intent as data (names + JSON args + ids); code must parse it, run the real function, and return results the stateless model can read on the next turn.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Branch on a non-empty tool_calls list, json.loads each arguments string, dispatch via registry.get(name), call fn(**args) inside try/except, and append {role:'tool', tool_call_id:id, content:str(result)} once per call.

theory.whyImportant: Dispatch is where model intent becomes real effect and where id-pairing, argument-parsing, and error-handling bugs concentrate, so doing it correctly is central to a working, resilient agent.
theory.realWorldExample: A support agent's turn returns two calls — get_order and issue_refund; the code parses each, runs both, and appends two tool messages keyed by their ids so the model sees exactly which result belongs to which action.

followUps.question: What if the model requests a tool that doesn't exist?
followUps.answer: registry.get returns None; return an error observation like "unknown tool 'x'" so the model can recover rather than raising a KeyError.

followUps.question: Why catch exceptions inside dispatch?
followUps.answer: So a failing tool becomes an error observation fed back to the model, keeping the loop alive instead of crashing the whole run.

theory.question: Why is the tool_call_id so important, and what breaks if it's wrong or missing?
theory.directAnswer: The tool_call_id is the join key the model uses to match each observation to the request that produced it. If it's wrong, the model may attribute a result to the wrong call; if a call gets no result message at all, the model sees a dangling request it expected an answer to. Both corrupt the conversation, and the damage is worst when several tools are called in one turn, since only the id disambiguates which result is which.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A unique identifier the model assigns to each tool call and expects echoed back on the corresponding tool-result message.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single turn can contain multiple tool calls, so the model needs an unambiguous way to pair each returned observation with its originating request.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You copy call['id'] into the tool-result message's tool_call_id, producing exactly one result message per id; skipping a call or reusing an id breaks the pairing the model relies on.

theory.whyImportant: Correct id pairing is what keeps multi-call turns coherent; without it the model's reasoning about what happened becomes unreliable.
theory.realWorldExample: An agent that ran three lookups in one turn but appended only two results left one call unanswered; the model re-requested it and looped until the dangling id was fixed by always appending one result per call.

followUps.question: Can you merge results for several calls into one message?
followUps.answer: No — each id needs its own tool-result message; a merged message loses the per-id pairing the model expects.

followUps.question: What if a provider omits ids?
followUps.answer: Some interfaces allow one call per turn without explicit ids, but for multi-call turns you rely on the ids; generate or track them yourself if the provider requires it.

scenario.question: Your agent intermittently loops re-requesting a tool it already 'called'. Multiple tools are used per turn. How do you debug it?
scenario.directAnswer: Inspect the transcript for a turn where the model requested N tools but the history has fewer than N tool-result messages, or where a tool_call_id in a result doesn't match any request. The usual cause is dropping a call when iterating (e.g. returning early on the first error) or mismatching ids, leaving a dangling request the model keeps re-asking. Fix by always appending exactly one id-matched result per call, converting errors to observations instead of returning early.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A dispatch bug where not every tool call in a multi-call turn gets a correctly-keyed result.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Early returns on error, exceptions escaping the per-call loop, or copying the wrong id cause missing or mismatched tool-result messages, and the model re-requests what it never saw answered.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Compare requested call ids to result tool_call_ids per turn; a mismatch or shortfall pinpoints the dropped/miskeyed call. Restructure dispatch so each call independently yields one result and errors become observations.

scenario.whyImportant: It highlights the most common multi-call dispatch defect and reinforces the one-result-per-id invariant that keeps the loop from spinning.
scenario.realWorldExample: A try/except around the whole loop caused the code to bail after the first failing call, so the second call's result was never appended; the model saw a dangling request and re-issued it every turn until dispatch was moved inside the per-call loop.

followUps.question: How do you make this invariant hard to violate?
followUps.answer: Structure the code to always emit one result per call and add a post-check asserting result ids equal request ids for the turn.

followUps.question: How would you catch it in production?
followUps.answer: Log requested-vs-answered call counts per turn and alert on any mismatch, which surfaces dropped or miskeyed results immediately.

coding.question: Write handle_tool_calls that parses, dispatches, and returns one id-matched tool-result message per call, handling bad JSON, unknown tools, and exceptions.
coding.thoughtProcess: The invariant is one result message per call id, in order, and never a crash. So I iterate each call, json.loads the arguments only if it's a string (catching JSONDecodeError as an error observation), resolve the name with registry.get to guard unknown tools, and wrap execution in try/except to turn failures into error text. Every branch ends by appending a message keyed by the call's id, guaranteeing the pairing.
lineByLine: Iterate every call so no request in a multi-call turn is dropped.
Parse arguments only when they are a string; malformed JSON becomes an error observation.
registry.get guards against a hallucinated tool name without raising.
The function runs inside try/except so a tool failure becomes error text, not a crash.
Each branch appends exactly one message keyed by call['id'], preserving the request↔result pairing.
The return is the list of tool-result messages the loop will add to history.
coding.timeComplexity: O(t) in the number of tool calls in the turn.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(t) for the result messages produced.

followUps.question: How would you validate arguments against a schema before executing?
followUps.answer: Parse into a pydantic args model per tool and, on ValidationError, produce an error observation instead of calling the function.

followUps.question: How does this change for parallel execution?
followUps.answer: Run the independent calls concurrently (threads/asyncio) and still append one id-matched result per call, preserving pairing — covered in the parallel-tool-calls topic.

keyTakeaways: The act phase is parse-and-dispatch: read tool_calls, parse each arguments blob, resolve the name in a registry, execute, and append a result.
Arguments usually arrive as a JSON string — json.loads defensively and turn malformed JSON into an error observation.
Guard unknown tool names and wrap execution in try/except so failures become recoverable observations, not crashes.
Every tool-result message must carry the original tool_call_id — the id pairs each observation to its request.
Handle every call in a multi-call turn: one id-matched result per call, or the model sees a dangling request and loops.
